strategy.title: Programa Espacial Mexicano 2026-2030
strategy.owner: Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones (ATDT), with the Agencia Espacial Mexicana as technical authority
strategy.summary: Published in the DOF on 4 June 2026 with the ATDT as issuing body, under the Plan Nacional de Desarrollo 2025-2030 and the ATDT sectoral programme. Its legal basis cites CPEUM arts. 26 and 28, the Ley de Planeación and the 28 Nov 2024 DOF decree that created the ATDT. Initial projects: a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities; a constellation of small Earth-observation satellites; a national centre to process satellite imagery; specialist training; and international cooperation, including ITU coordination of orbital positions and spectrum. The AEM is the technical authority, and the programme states that the AEM had not yet produced a current strategic programme in its institutional phase.
strategy.budget: No dedicated budget figure for the 2026-2030 programme is stated in the programme text. Press (Expansión, 8 Jan 2026, citing the 2026 PEF) reports a federal allocation to the AEM of 46,755 millones de pesos, down 33.1% from 69,950 millones in 2025. The unit and the PEF annex are not verified; a separate press report gives a different scale. Treat as press-reported, unit unresolved.
goals: Build a new national telecommunications satellite to connect remote localities
Deploy a constellation of small Earth observation satellites for civil protection, environment, agriculture, security and territorial planning
Create a national centre to process and analyse satellite imagery from national and commercial systems
Train Mexican specialists for the space sector
Link Mexico to the international space sector and strengthen management of orbital positions and spectrum rights at the ITU
strategy.law: No comprehensive national space activities law found in the sources opened. Founding statute: Ley que crea la Agencia Espacial Mexicana (DOF 30 Jul 2010), which creates the AEM as a decentralised public body; its 2010 sector reference (SCT) is superseded by the ATDT sectorisation stated in the 2026 programme. Constitutional basis: CPEUM art. 28 (satellite communication as a priority area under State rectory) and art. 26 (planning).

strategy.title: National Space Science and Technology Policy (2021)
strategy.status: in force (implementation period 2021/22 to 2029/30; reaffirmed by government, Mar 2026)
strategy.owner: Ministry of Education, Innovation, Youth, Sport, Arts and Culture (implementation lead); NCRST (coordinating agency). Issued in 2021 by MHETI.
strategy.summary: Namibia's Cabinet adopted the policy on 23 March 2021 (Cabinet no. 4TH/23.03.21/006), launched 4 June 2021. It has four objectives: awareness; collaboration and funding; human and institutional capacity; access and use of space technology. Cabinet approved drafting a Space Science and Technology Bill in 2025 (press). A national steering committee ran public consultations in 2026 (NBC). No enacted law or space agency was found; the government reaffirmed the policy in March 2026.
strategy.budget: The policy's implementation plan (appendix) has a budget column in N$ thousands per activity; the totals were not extracted. No separate national space budget line was found in the sources opened. The 2026/27 education budget (press) includes N$25.5m for a satellite data ground receiving station at the Windhoek Telecom earth station, a separate site; not confirmed as space budget in an official document. NUST station: government-funded (SIA, Mar 2026), amount not stated.
goals: Improve awareness and appreciation of space science and technology in Namibia (Objective 1)
Ensure collaboration and mobilisation of resources for funding space science and technology (Objective 2)
Build human and institutional capacity in space science and technology (Objective 3)
Ensure optimal access to and use of space technologies (Objective 4)
strategy.law: No space law enacted in sources opened. Space Science and Technology Bill: Cabinet approved drafting (Aug 2025, press); National Steering Committee consultations in 2026 (NBC). Not tabled in Parliament as far as found. Legal basis of NCRST: Research, Science and Technology Act, 2004 (Act 23 of 2004), as cited in the 2021 policy.

strategy.summary: Nigeria's National Space Policy was approved in 2000, and a 25-year implementation roadmap was endorsed in 2005, phased from government-funded development toward commercialization and public-private partnership. Several targets slipped, including a first Nigerian astronaut (originally 2015, later restated for 2030) and a full launch capability. At its first meeting in March 2026, the National Space Council set up an expert working group to revise the 25-year roadmap, with the implementation cost to go to the Federal Executive Council.

government.notes: Civil space policy is coordinated by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy, which signs space policy letters on behalf of the education and defense ministers. ESA subscriptions are split by budget line, with Economic Affairs funding Basic Activities and most optional programs, Education funding Science, and Defence adding conditional one-off contributions counted toward the NATO spending norm. The Netherlands Space Agency, administratively part of RVO, advises and executes under a steering committee of the sponsoring ministries. Parliament shapes funding through ministry budgets, and any permanent increase beyond the one-off 2025 top-up was left to the current cabinet.

strategy.summary: The Long-Term Space Agenda, prepared on the advice of the Netherlands Space Office and endorsed by the cabinet in February 2025, replaced the earlier three-year policy cycle tied to ESA ministerial conferences. It sets six missions spanning security, climate, science, satellite data, industry and international law. A 2017 to 2024 policy evaluation found the missions insufficiently concrete, and in January 2026 the cabinet committed to prioritize them. The Netherlands Space Office was renamed the Netherlands Space Agency in March 2026 with a stronger mandate.

government.notes: Space policy and regulation sit in one portfolio, with the Minister for Space acting as both policy lead and statutory licensing decision-maker, advised by MBIE and the New Zealand Space Agency (led by an acting General Manager, Space, Andrew Johnson, per the August 2026 briefing). Funding is small and largely flows through MBIE appropriations, Cabinet reprioritizations and the Catalyst Fund rather than a dedicated space budget. Security agencies screen license applications and the 2025 amendment added national security powers over ground stations. The portfolio changed hands twice in 2026 (Chris Penk from 7 April, Paul Goldsmith from 13 August), and a general election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 with official results due 27 November 2026, so the incumbent Luxon government continues until a new government is formed.

strategy.summary: Oman's National Space Policy and Executive Program is a ten year framework for 2023 to 2033 that aims to make Oman a regional hub for space applications. It rests on four pillars (economic diversification, national security, capacity building and environmental stewardship) and prioritizes the downstream sector as the entry point. Implementation runs in three phases, from preparation and legal frameworks, to priority projects, to expansion and sustainability, through 14 key projects and 8 quick wins. The ministry reported that 2023 to 2025 achievements included growth to about 26 space companies and over 400 sector jobs.

strategy.summary: Pakistan's first National Space Policy was approved by the federal cabinet in December 2023 and sets the country's first legal and regulatory framework for space activities. It frames space as a tool for socioeconomic development and national security, commits to peaceful use, and opens the market to public-private partnerships and foreign low Earth orbit communications providers. SUPARCO implements, monitors and revises the policy, and the Pakistan Space Activities Regulatory Board licenses operators under rules issued in 2024. The policy sits beside the longer running Space Program 2040, which drives a fast satellite launch cadence built mainly with Chinese partners.

strategy.summary: The Philippine Space Act, approved on 8 August 2019, embeds the Philippine Space Development and Utilization Policy and created the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) as the central body for space policy and programs. The policy aims to make the country space-capable and space-faring within a decade, organized around six key development areas. strategy.budget: At the ESA Ministerial Council in Bremen in November 2025 Poland declared nearly EUR 550 million for ESA optional programs for 2026 to 2028, within a total ESA commitment reported at EUR 731 million. The MikroSAR military radar satellite contract (May 2025) is worth about PLN 860 million gross. The Łukasiewicz Network space research program, including a small launcher, is estimated at PLN 2.4 billion over about ten years.
goals: Reach a 3 percent share of European space sector turnover by 2030
Develop satellite applications for the digital economy and public administration
Build security and defense capabilities based on space technologies
Create favorable legal and institutional conditions for the space sector
Develop the skilled workforce the sector needs
strategy.law: Act on Space Activities of 13 February 2026 (Dz.U. 2026 item 465), published 3 April 2026. The POLSA President issues licenses and keeps the National Register of Space Objects, the minister responsible for the economy is the appeal authority, and the Minister of National Defence is competent for activities of units under that minister.

strategy.summary: Portugal Space 2030 was approved by the Council of Ministers on 15 February 2018 together with the draft Space Law, and set the national strategy for space to 2030. It aims to grow a space economy built on data, services and infrastructure, using the Atlantic position of the Azores for launch, return and ground station activities. In 2025 the government set up a Space Interministerial Working Group that shaped a record ESA subscription, and the 2026 agenda centers on the Santa Maria spaceport, reentry operations and the Atlantic Constellation with Spain. No formal successor strategy had been published as of this file.

strategy.summary: Rwanda's National Space Policy, dated March 2025, sets the goal of a resilient space sector by 2035 that contributes to economic growth and quality of life. strategy.summary: Singapore has not published a national space strategy document. The policy basis is the mandate of the National Space Agency of Singapore (NSAS), established on 1 April 2026 under the trade and industry ministry, which took over the Office for Space Technology and Industry (OSTIn) and has five pillars: national space capabilities, R&D, industry, international partnerships and space legislation. Operational guidance comes from the 2024 Guidelines for Singapore Related Space Activities, and funding from the S$210 million Space Technology Development Program set aside since 2022. Official statements say Singapore does not prioritize launch capability because of land constraints.

government.notes: Serbia has no space agency, so space decisions run through the Government and individual ministries, with the Ministry of Science as the de facto lead and funder through its research budget. International commitments are driven by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Artemis Accords, 2026) and sector bodies (RHMZ for EUMETSAT, BioSense for Copernicus). The political setting is in flux: President Vucic resigned on 27 September 2026 to run for Prime Minister, Speaker Ana Brnabic is acting President, the National Assembly is dissolved ahead of the 25 October 2026 snap election, and a presidential election must follow within three months. Prime Minister Djuro Macut (in office since 16 April 2025) leads the government until a new one is formed.

The agency's 2027 to 2029 budget request proposes SEK 2.08 billion for appropriation 3:4 Space research and space activities in 2027, rising to about SEK 2.95 billion in 2029. The 2026 spring amending budget added SEK 400 million, with SEK 386 million in equity for SSC launch capability at Esrange and SEK 14 million for licensing at the Swedish National Space Agency. Military space is funded separately through the Armed Forces space billion for 2024 to 2032 and a SEK 1.3 billion military satellite package announced in January 2026.
goals: Promote peaceful and sustainable use of space and help develop international rules, including on space debris

Keep space legislation supportive of domestic activity, international obligations and private investment

government.notes: Space policy is set by the National Space Policy Committee, chaired by a Deputy Prime Minister with the digital economy ministry providing the secretariat, and its decisions go to the Cabinet for approval. Implementation and most space funding sit with GISTDA and NARIT under the higher education and science ministry, through the annual budget act passed by parliament. Spectrum and orbital filings are handled by the independent NBTC. Following the 8 February 2026 general election, the House re-elected Anutin Charnvirakul as Prime Minister on 19 March 2026 and the King endorsed his second cabinet on 31 March 2026.

goals: Develop a domestic space economy and industry that supports national security, prosperity and sustainability
Sustain national Earth observation capacity through the THEOS satellite series operated by GISTDA

strategy.summary: The Cabinet approved the 15-year National Space Master Plan 2023-2037 in December 2022, alongside a National Communication Satellite Policy. The plan aims to build a space economy that supports national security, prosperity and sustainability through eight strategies covering security, economy and industry, innovation, technology, exploration and international cooperation. In July 2025 the National Space Policy Committee gave initial approval to a revised master plan that incorporates recommendations from the National Economic and Social Development Council and still requires formal approval.

strategy.summary: Taiwan's space policy is set by the Phase III National Space Program, announced in 2019 for 2019 to 2028 with an expected cost of NT$25.1 billion and a target of at least one satellite launch per year. It shifts Taiwan from single satellites to constellations, with domestic optical, SAR and low Earth orbit communications satellites, launch vehicles and a national launch site. The Taiwan Space Agency, an administrative corporation under the National Science and Technology Council, implements the program. TASA describes its two main goals as strengthening national security and promoting the space industry.

strategy.summary: Decision 169/QD-TTg, signed by the Prime Minister on 4 February 2021, sets Vietnam's space science and technology strategy through 2030 and builds on the 2006 national space technology strategy. It targets a mid-level position in space science and technology in Southeast Asia by 2030, mastery of small high-resolution Earth observation satellite technology, replacement of the VINASAT communication satellites and a large expansion of the space workforce. At the March 2026 inauguration of the Vietnam National Space Center, the government restated these targets and said it is moving toward a national space law.

USA-NJ.profile: New Jersey has limited space activity, centered on university research. The New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark runs the Center for Solar-Terrestrial Research and an Institute for Space Weather Sciences, and Rowan University in Glassboro was the first New Jersey university to send a satellite to space under a NASA CubeSat program. The New Jersey Economic Development Authority is developing an $8.6 million Aerospace Innovation Center in Atlantic County, focused mainly on aviation.

USA-NM.name: New Mexico
USA-NM.profile: New Mexico owns Spaceport America, operated by the New Mexico Spaceport Authority, where Virgin Galactic expects its first Delta-class spaceship for flight testing in late 2026 and commercial flights in 2027, and where Hermeus and other customers test vehicles. NASA's White Sands Test Facility and White Sands Missile Range support propulsion testing and flight operations. Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque hosts the AFRL Space Vehicles Directorate and the Space Rapid Capabilities Office, alongside Sandia and Los Alamos national laboratories and Rocket Lab's space solar cell production, which received CHIPS Act funding.

USA-NV.profile: Nevada has limited space activity. Aerospace and defense contractor Sierra Nevada Corporation, parent of Sierra Space, is headquartered in Sparks, and the University of Nevada, Reno joined the US Space Command Academic Engagement Enterprise in 2024. In 2026 state leaders, including the lieutenant governor, discussed a bid to host NASA's planned US Space Academy, and a private company, United Spaceports, has proposed a spaceport between Las Vegas and Pahrump.

USA-NY.name: New York
USA-NY.profile: New York has no NASA field center or launch site, and its space activity is led by industry and universities. L3Harris designs and builds high resolution imaging payloads for government and commercial satellites in Rochester, and Moog completed a major expansion of its space actuation and avionics manufacturing in East Aurora in 2025. NASA ended the lease of the Goddard Institute for Space Studies at Columbia University in 2025, and its staff have worked remotely since June 2025. Beyond Reach Labs opened a 16,000 square foot Brooklyn facility for deployable spacecraft solar arrays in September 2026.

USA-OH.name: Ohio
USA-OH.profile: Ohio's space role centers on NASA Glenn Research Center in Cleveland and Brook Park, which leads propulsion, power and communications research, and its Neil Armstrong Test Facility near Sandusky, home of the Space Environments Complex. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base hosts Air Force Research Laboratory headquarters, the National Air and Space Intelligence Center and the Space Force's National Space Intelligence Center, activated in 2022. Glenn and the Armstrong Test Facility employed about 600 fewer civil servants and contractors in January 2026 than a year earlier after buyouts and contract cancellations. In September 2026 Governor DeWine formed a steering group, chaired by the Ohio Department of Development, to pursue the planned U.S. Space Academy.

The Oklahoma Space Industry Development Authority manages the site and became part of the Oklahoma Department of Aerospace and Aeronautics on July 1, 2025, under Senate Bill 912. Dawn Aerospace has agreed to base its US operations at the spaceport and plans suborbital flights from 2027.

The state supported Astrobotic's Pittsburgh expansion in 2023 with more than $4 million through the Department of Community and Economic Development. In July 2026 Voyager Technologies and Penn State signed a memorandum of understanding on in-space research, manufacturing and national security technology.

Brown Space Engineering, a student group, has built and flown CubeSats. The state's defense and ocean technology cluster around Naval Undersea Warfare Center Newport is focused on undersea rather than space systems.

USA-SC.name: South Carolina
USA-SC.profile: South Carolina has no NASA center, military space command, launch site or spaceport, and its space activity is concentrated in universities. The South Carolina Space Grant Consortium is based at the College of Charleston, whose students' ultraviolet imaging payload flew to the International Space Station in April 2026 and whose CubeSat payload launched in July 2026. Coastal Carolina University is building the state's first university-run CubeSat and requested $450,000 in state funds for its launch in January 2026, and Clemson University signed a Space Act Agreement with NASA Johnson Space Center in April 2024. The state's large aerospace manufacturing base, including Boeing South Carolina and the Lockheed Martin F-16 line in Greenville, is focused on aircraft rather than space.

The University of Tennessee Space Institute, a University of Tennessee graduate campus beside the base, conducts aerospace and hypersonics research. Oak Ridge National Laboratory produces plutonium-238 for radioisotope power systems on NASA missions.

USA-TX.profile: Texas hosts NASA's Johnson Space Center and a human spaceflight and lunar industry cluster in Houston, including Intuitive Machines at the Houston Spaceport. SpaceX builds and launches Starship at Starbase, which incorporated as a city in May 2025, and tests engines at McGregor, while Blue Origin operates its New Shepard launch site near Van Horn and Firefly Aerospace is headquartered in Cedar Park. The Texas Space Commission, created in 2023, awards grants from the Space Exploration and Aeronautics Research Fund and funded the 200 million dollar Texas A&M Space Institute at NASA's Exploration Park next to Johnson Space Center, scheduled to open in fall 2026.

USA-VA.profile: Virginia hosts NASA Langley Research Center in Hampton and NASA Wallops Flight Facility on the Eastern Shore, where the state-owned Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport supports Rocket Lab and Northrop Grumman launches. Rocket Lab opened Launch Complex 3 for its Neutron rocket in August 2025, and the first Neutron launch, targeted for late 2026, could slip into 2027. National security space leadership is concentrated in Northern Virginia, including U.S. Space Force headquarters at the Pentagon and the National Reconnaissance Office in Chantilly. USA-WA.name: Washington
USA-WA.office: Washington State Department of Commerce (staffs the Washington Space Council created by Executive Order 26-04 in 2026)
USA-WA.profile: Washington is a major commercial space hub around Seattle, with Blue Origin and Stoke Space headquartered in Kent, SpaceX Starlink satellite production in Redmond (about 70 satellites per week in early 2026, per SpaceX's IPO filing) and Amazon Leo satellite production in Kirkland. Redmond's in-space propulsion campus became part of Rocketdyne in August 2026 when AE Industrial Partners closed its purchase of a majority stake in L3Harris's space propulsion and power business, and newer firms include Portal Space Systems in Bothell and Starcloud and Gravitics in the Redmond area. In September 2026 Governor Ferguson created the 23-member Washington Space Council by Executive Order 26-04, staffed by the state Department of Commerce.

Sierra Space operates a propulsion and space systems site in the Madison area (the former Orbital Technologies Corporation), which won a $20.2 million Air Force Research Laboratory contract in 2022 for an advanced upper stage rocket engine.
